prompt: Explain the Mpemba effect, the claim that hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water, and why physicists still argue about whether it is real.
Using an everyday analogy, explain how a laser produces light in which every wave marches in step, through stimulated emission and population inversion.
Describe, vividly and for a general audience, how a tokamak confines a plasma hotter than the core of the Sun using twisted magnetic fields.
Explain why the sky glows red and orange at sunset, tracing how Rayleigh scattering changes as sunlight crosses more of the atmosphere.
Explain the Casimir effect, in which two uncharged metal plates in a vacuum are pushed together, and what it suggests about empty space.
Explain how a sonic boom forms when an aircraft breaks the sound barrier, and why the boom follows the plane rather than happening once.
Explain how the arctic tern migrates from pole to pole every year, seeing more daylight than any other animal, and how it navigates.
Describe in a whimsical tone how a cuckoo chick tricks its foster parents into feeding it while it pushes their own eggs out of the nest.
Explain how the immortal jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to an earlier stage of its life cycle, and what that does and does not mean for ageing.
Explain quorum sensing, the way bacteria count their own numbers with chemical signals and switch on behaviours like glowing only when crowded.
Write a haunting description of the deep-sea anglerfish, its glowing lure and the strange way males fuse permanently to females.
Make the case, in a reflective tone, that Pascal's wager fails once you notice how many possible gods there could be.
Explain the problem of moral luck, using the example of two equally careless drivers where only one happens to hit a child.
Explain the sorites paradox, asking how many grains of sand you can remove before a heap stops being a heap, and what it says about vague words.
Explain Nick Bostrom's paperclip maximizer thought experiment and the worry about AI goals that it is meant to illustrate.
Write a short, lyrical story about a lighthouse keeper who discovers that the light has been signalling to something out at sea.
Write a poetic description of a city during the first heavy snowfall of the year, seen from the window of a night train.
Write a melancholy vignette about the last speaker of a language recording a lullaby for a linguist.
Explain Benford's law, the surprising fact that in many real-world datasets the leading digit 1 appears about 30% of the time, and how auditors use it to spot fraud.
Explain the four colour theorem, which says any map needs at most four colours so neighbours differ, and why its 1976 computer-assisted proof was controversial.
Explain the birthday paradox, showing why only 23 people are needed for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday.
Describe the Great Molasses Flood of 1919 in Boston, when a storage tank burst and a wave of syrup swept through the streets.
Describe the Tunguska event of 1908, when an explosion flattened 80 million trees across the Siberian forest without leaving a crater.
Describe the Dancing Plague of 1518 in Strasbourg, when hundreds of people danced for days, and the theories offered to explain it.
Explain public-key cryptography using the analogy of a padlock that anyone can close but only one person can open.
Explain how a Bloom filter can tell you that an item is definitely not in a set, or only probably in it, while using very little memory.
Explain the Dunning-Kruger effect and why people with the least skill in an area are often the most confident about it.
Explain the spotlight effect, our tendency to overestimate how much other people notice our appearance and mistakes.
Explain the lipstick effect, the idea that consumers keep buying small luxuries during recessions, and why economists debate whether it is real.
Explain the cobra effect, named after a colonial bounty on snakes in Delhi, as an example of incentives that backfire.
